extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors as reference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and supporting 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility rejections, including how to identify judicial exceptions in claims, evaluate additional claim elements under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A Prong One/Two and Step 2B), and use required evidentiary support and form paragraphs in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner has determined the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP §2106.04(a)(2). Alternatively, provide justification under the “tentative abstract idea” procedure (MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)). Explanations may cite appropriate court decisions but examiners should be familiar with cited decisions and avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match. Sample provided: identify claim step of comparing information to a threshold as an abstract mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain laws of nature or natural phenomena recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify that law or phenomenon as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106.04(b) for more information. Sample explanations: (1) claim recites a correlation that is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body; (2) claim recites X which is a natural phenomenon because it occurs in nature and exists apart from human action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain product-of-nature exceptions (markedly different characteristics analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106.04(b) and §2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample explanation: recited isolated X is compared to its naturally occurring counterpart; if no indication that isolation resulted in marked difference in structure/function/properties, then X is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do or do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation should address additional elements both individually and in combination using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§2106.04(d) and 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity. If appropriate, the examiner should explain why additional elements do integrate or provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do or do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner has concluded particular limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection must expressly support that conclusion in writing with one of the evidentiary options in Subsection III. Address whether a new combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception (Diamond v. Diehr); a combination of well-known elements may nevertheless amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection threshold: only when readily apparent based on examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner’s expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries that the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. If appropriate, explain why additional elements integrate an exception or provide an inventive concept. See MPEP §2106.07(c) for clarifying the record when a claim is found eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting assertion that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (evidentiary requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the following options (A–D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option A: citation to express statement in the specification or applicant’s prosecution statement demonstrating routine/conventional nature (specification describing element as well-understood/routine/conventional or commercially available). Option B: citation to one or more court decisions that note the conventional nature of the element(s), ensuring the claim limitations match those in the decisions and are recited at the same high level of generality. Option C: citation to a publication (book/manual/review article) demonstrating the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field; the publication must show prevalence comparable to elements that need not be described in detail to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Option D: official notice by the examiner that the element is widely prevalent or in common use, used only when examiner is certain based on personal knowledge; procedures for taking official notice are in MPEP §2144.03. Avoid relying solely on specification silence to find an element conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary posture for Step 2A Prong One (no requirement for external evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception without relying on external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement to rely on publications, affidavits, or declarations to find a claim recites a judicial exception. Courts have affirmed identification of abstract ideas without evidence. However, factual showings may be required when asserting elements are well-understood, routine, conventional in Step 2B (see Subsection III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer functions and how to treat them
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data), examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind that courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic computer components in combination perform functions that are not merely generic (DDR Holdings). See MPEP §2106.05(f) for information about generic computing functions courts have found to be mere instructions to implement a judicial exception on a computer, and MPEP §2106.05(d) for information about well-understood, routine, conventional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and mere field-of-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or that merely link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process that computes a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation; limiting an abstract idea to a particular industry (as in Parker v. Flook) is insufficient to supply an inventive concept. See MPEP §2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and §2106.05(h) for general linking to a technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address additional elements both individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing whether a claim integrates an exception into a practical application or amounts to significantly more, the explanation should address additional elements both individually and as a combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new combination of steps may be patent eligible even though all steps were individually known (Diamond v. Diehr). Therefore it is critical to consider whether the combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception (see MPEP §2106.05).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the specification and suggest claim amendments when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action as suggestions to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps compact prosecution and assists applicants in overcoming eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specified form paragraphs and required content for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017) for §101 rejections and follow the ordering and bracketed-content instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: form paragraph 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions/final rejections. Form paragraph 7.05 should be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using other form paragraphs. Form paragraph 7.05.016 (Nonstatutory directed to judicial exception without inventive concept) requires bracketed content: [1] identify whether claim directed to law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea; [2] identify the exception by referring to how recited in claim and explain why considered an exception (e.g., identify abstract-idea grouping); [3] explain why combination of additional elements fails to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; [4] explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If the exception is a tentative abstract idea, include form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in citing court decisions as evidence of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on court decisions to support that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional, ensure the claim limitations under examination are the same as those found conventional by the courts and are recited at the same high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough that the additional elements are similar to elements in those cases. Also, court decisions referenced are not meant to imply all computer functions are conventional or that claims reciting generic computer components are necessarily ineligible; DDR Holdings illustrates exceptions. See MPEP §2106.05(d) and §2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete examination under other patentability requirements despite §101 rejections (compact prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under principles of compact prosecution, regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and utility/inventorship/double patenting and non-statutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
